introduction: The Covenant of Bahá’u’lláh is his written appointment of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá as the Centre to whom all should turn and the sole interpreter of his word, with the House of Justice to legislate after. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains it here almost entirely by one purpose, unity: without a centre every strong opinion becomes a sect, “as was the case in former ages,” and a religion meant to unite the world cannot itself be divided. Firmness therefore means obedience, and the last reading sets beside it the duty of independent investigation and the admission that no one has a full understanding. Christian history is the main comparison, as it is for ‘Abdu’l-Bahá: “upon this rock,” “feed my sheep,” the factions at Corinth, the council at Jerusalem, Paul withstanding Peter. The Qur’án’s cable, Cyprian, the Iroquois Tree of the Great Peace and the First Vatican Council’s definition of papal authority are here too. The objections come from Kant, Milton, Mill, Jefferson and Madison, who trusted free opinion, and from the Talmud’s “It is not in heaven.”
questions: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says there were dissensions after Christ “because there was no Center.” Read “upon this rock,” “feed my sheep” and Paul’s rebuke of Peter. What was given to Peter, and what was left unsettled?
“No one should say ‘my opinion is this.’” The last reading says each person must investigate and strive for greater understanding. Name the matters to which each sentence applies.

Mill and Milton hold that truth needs open disagreement. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says “when there is difference of view there is absence of the Spirit.” What kind of difference is he speaking of, and what does Bahá’í consultation do with differing views?

Compare the Centre of the Covenant with the papacy as defined in 1870, and with the rabbis’ rule by majority in “It is not in heaven.” What are three different answers to the question, who decides what the text means?
Madison thought many sects protect freedom. Why do the readings treat even one division as fatal to the purpose of this Faith?
“‘Abdu’l-Bahá loves all no matter how they turn away from Him,” and the firm are told to give Covenant-breakers no room. How are both held?

outside.why: A Zoroastrian, a Siyyid, a mullá, a Jew and a Christian “are accounted as one spirit.” Paul of the first churches: there is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.
It was “an impossibility.” The Qur’án of the tribes of Arabia: if thou hadst spent all that is in the earth thou couldst not have attuned their hearts, but Allah hath attuned them.
Under the Covenant “separation hath no reality.” Paul: neither death, nor life, nor height, nor depth, shall be able to separate us from the love of God.
“The melody is the melody of unity.” A psalm: behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!

Shield souls “from veiled suggestions and secret whisperings”; otherwise “a new sect would emerge each day.” Paul: mark them which cause divisions and offences contrary to the doctrine which ye have learned.
The purpose was “to gather all existent beings around one point.” Jesus: there shall be one fold, and one shepherd.
Cyprian of Carthage, about 250, on a unity with one source: as there are many rays of the sun, but one light; and many branches of a tree, but one strength based in its tenacious root.
The Covenant is for protection, for spreading the Faith, and for “the brotherhood of the East and the West.” Paul: one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all.
“The greatest of all affairs is the unity and oneness of the friends of God.” Jesus’ prayer the night before he died: that they all may be one.
He “hath made manifest the Eternal Covenant.” Jeremiah: behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that I will make a new covenant.

The Law, “the covenant of which Thou hast established with all Thy Prophets.” The Qur’án: when Allah made His covenant with the prophets: afterward there will come unto you a messenger; ye shall believe in him and ye shall help him.

Bahá’u’lláh “appointed the Centre towards whom all must turn.” The Gospel text nearest to such an appointment: thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven.

This Dispensation leaves “no room for discord” because the Centre was named in writing. Within a few years of Jesus’ words to Peter, Paul could write: I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed. What did the earlier appointment leave undefined that a written Covenant settles?
“In every cycle … an implicit statement was made.” The risen Jesus to Peter, three times: feed my lambs; feed my sheep.
Another implicit provision for the time after: I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever.

In the past “every man with a new idea” attributed it to God. Corinth, about twenty-five years after the crucifixion: every one of you saith, I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas. Is Christ divided?
A Centre and a House of Justice whose decisions “must be accepted.” The Letter to the Hebrews: obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls.

Whatever the House of Justice prescribes must be accepted, and “all such doors are closed.” John Stuart Mill argued that no body may close them: if all mankind minus one were of one opinion, mankind would be no more justified in silencing that one person. What does Mill fear, and what in the next reading answers part of it?
Bahá’u’lláh enjoined “non-interference in matters of belief and conscience.” The Universal Declaration: everyone has the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion.

An authorized interpreter, an elected legislature, and freedom of conscience. A peacemaker of the Thirty Years’ War proposed a similar division: in essentials unity, in non-essentials liberty, in all things charity.
“The doors of contention must be barred.” Paul: that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind.

If there are “differences as to the meaning of the Book,” turn to the Centre. When the first Christians disagreed over the Law, they went up to Jerusalem unto the apostles and elders about this question.
Otherwise “each soul will interpret the divine verses according to their own desire.” The Second Letter of Peter: no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.

Act on the apparent meaning and turn to one interpreter. In a famous story the rabbis refuse even a voice from heaven in a legal dispute and decide by majority: It is not in heaven. And God, told of it, laughs: My children have triumphed over Me. What does each tradition trust to keep interpretation from running wild?

Either Bahá’u’lláh erred in commanding obedience to the Centre, or one must obey. A Roman officer saw authority in the same chain: I also am a man set under authority; I say unto one, Go, and he goeth.

“No one should say ‘my opinion is this.’” Kant called it immaturity to need another’s direction: Sapere aude! Have courage to use your own understanding. In what matters do the readings ask a believer to set his opinion aside, and in what matters does the last reading tell him to use it?

The Covenant exists “so that no one should give his own opinion.” Milton thought a people seeking truth needs many: opinion in good men is but knowledge in the making. Is there a way for opinion to be offered that the Covenant does not forbid?
“There were dissensions in the time of Christ because there was no Center.” The apostles’ first act alone was to fill an empty place, and they did it by drawing lots.
So that no one “might say anything on his own behalf.” Jesus of the Spirit of truth: he shall not speak of himself; but whatsoever he shall hear, that shall he speak.
“You see how many sects and religions appeared after Christ.” The Qur’án on what follows every revelation: they have broken their religion among them into sects, each group rejoicing in its tenets.

“The point to which all eyes should turn is One.” The Roman Catholic Church gave that place a definition in 1870: the Roman Pontiff, when he speaks ex cathedra, is possessed of infallibility. How is the Centre of the Covenant like and unlike this, in how the authority was given and in how far it reaches?
“All others save the Center of the Covenant are equal.” Jesus: one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren.
To turn to the Covenant “is to obey the Blessed Beauty.” The Qur’án of those who pledged themselves to Muḥammad: those who swear allegiance unto thee swear allegiance only unto Allah.
“Do not disrupt Bahá’í unity.” The Qur’án: hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá cites the saying to Peter. The words: upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.

Without the Centre “the Bahá’ís would be divided into a thousand sects.” Madison thought a multitude of sects was itself the protection of liberty. Why is a division that Madison welcomes in a nation a disaster in a religion whose purpose is the unity of mankind?

“A thousand different sects as was the case in former ages.” Francis Bacon, after a century of European religious war: heresies and schisms are of all others the greatest scandals; nothing doth so much keep men out of the Church as breach of unity.
“Each soul would find a particular opinion, and the Cause of God would be totally obliterated.” Jesus: every city or house divided against itself shall not stand.
Unity depends on “adherence to the writings of the Expounder.” Paul to Timothy: keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings.
“The foundation of the religion of God will not be shaken.” Jesus: the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell not: for it was founded upon a rock.
“The first condition is firmness in the Covenant.” Moses: the faithful God, which keepeth covenant and mercy with them that love him.
“You must be firm as mountains.” Paul: be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord.
Blessing on the firm and “woe and desolation” on violators. Hosea: they like men have transgressed the covenant: there have they dealt treacherously against me.
“If some ungrateful person should assault this pillar.” A psalm on betrayal from inside: mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me.
“Ye have striven to keep the Word whole and one.” Jesus to Peter: I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren.

Dissensions arise in religions “after the ascension” of their Founders. Paul, leaving Ephesus for the last time: after my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you; also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things.

All matters are referred to the House of Justice. Saxe’s blind men with their elephant show why reference is needed, and something else as well: each was partly in the right, and all were in the wrong. Can a community keep what is partly right in each view while one body decides?

“When there is difference of view there is absence of the Spirit.” Mill thought suppressing difference a presumption: all silencing of discussion is an assumption of infallibility. The Bahá’í writings elsewhere praise the clash of differing opinions in consultation. How is that reconciled with this sentence?
“God’s Will is independent of human opinion.” Isaiah: my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways.
The Covenant was made “for obedience and not for opposition.” Samuel to a king who had improved on his instructions: to obey is better than sacrifice.
Be so firm that Covenant-breakers “cannot draw a breath” where you are. The First Letter of John on those who left: they went out from us, but they were not of us.
They are “like Judas Iscariot … soon … forgotten like the foam of the sea.” Matthew: what will ye give me, and I will deliver him unto you? And they covenanted with him for thirty pieces of silver.
“Every sturdy ship must encounter massive waves.” The disciples in the storm: and he arose, and rebuked the wind, and said unto the sea, Peace, be still.
“If all the world should combine to overthrow the Covenant, it could not succeed.” Isaiah: the mountains shall depart, and the hills be removed; but the covenant of my peace shall not be removed.
“Reinforce the backs of the defenders of Thy Covenant.” When Moses’ arms grew heavy in the battle, Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side.

“Gathered beneath the shade of the Tree of the Covenant.” The Great Law of the Iroquois Confederacy uses the same image for a covenant among nations: roots have spread out from the Tree of the Great Peace, and any nation may trace them and take shelter beneath it.

An instrument “to direct and canalize these forces … after His ascension.” Jesus: I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now; when the Spirit of truth is come, he will guide you into all truth.
The Covenant “fixed on an inviolable basis.” A psalm in God’s voice: my covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips.
Individuals who “through the assertion of their own wills” would divide the faithful. Korah to Moses: ye take too much upon you, seeing all the congregation are holy, every one of them.
The Covenants are “the hub of the Bahá’í wheel.” Marcus Aurelius on what leaving the hub means: a branch cut off from the adjacent branch must of necessity be cut off from the whole tree also.

Without the Covenant the Faith “would be torn to pieces by the conflicting opinions of scholars.” Jefferson trusted open argument to make such conflict harmless: error of opinion may be tolerated where reason is left free to combat it. Why might a religion need more than that, and what does it risk in asking for more?

The Covenant protects against those “convinced that only their understanding of the Teachings is the right one.” Hillel: do not separate yourself from the community; do not trust in yourself until the day of your death.
“Independent investigation of truth” remains each person’s duty. Paul: prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
The Bereans were called noble for it: they searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.

“No human being can have a full and correct understanding of the revelation of God.” Augustine on readers who disagree about a verse: why not rather as both, if both be true? How does this humility about one’s own reading fit with turning to one authorized interpreter?
